newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Embattled Philippines fights off Thai spectre.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Philippines fights off Thai spectre.

text.p: The Philippines, unnerved by tumbling share prices and attacks on its currency, raised interest rates to their highest level in over two years on Friday as fears of a Thailand-like crisis swept across the country's financial markets.
The Central Bank was forced to raise overnight interest rates a startling seven percent to their highest level since March 1995, and dumped dollars to prop up the peso.

The intervention appeared to succeed but in Manila's share market the picture was one of more gloom as the index sunk to its lowest in 17 months, falling just over two percent to its lowest close in a year at 2,576.13 points.
"This is the sentiment around the region. It's not just the Philippines. But it's quite unfair to compare us with Thailand," said Philippine TA Securities economist Rolando Valenzuela.
It is the second time since April that the Philippines, the newest of Southeast Asia's rising economic stars, has watched its markets battered by the problems of Thailand.
Last month, foreign investors pulled out of the stock market in droves, fearful that the country was about to copy Thailand's earlier property and banking problems.
This time, it was again Thailand where financial and political worries have made investors jittery about the outlook for the region as a whole.

The peso firmed to 26.37 to the dollar only after the central bank again dumped dollars and boosted overnight interest rates to 20 percent -- almost double in the past month -- in the most active currency market in Manila on record, with over $650 million changing hands by the close.
And Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza warned speculators not to try to out-guess the government.
"The market is speculating we'll lower the overnight rate on Monday...But we'll keep it at that level until the market is no longer speculating," he told Reuters.
Edeza admitted that the Bank had been intervening in the market, buying and selling the dollar, but overall it was a net seller of the U.S. currency.
Government officials continued to insist that the Philippine economy, which has only started to shine just as the region's allure has begun to dim, was fundamentally sound.
Some fresh figures for March on Friday did give support to their claims. The trade deficit and growth in domestic credit and money supply all fell in the month.

Economists especially warmed to a marked slowdown in the growth of the country's trade deficit, which rose just 8.4 percent to $2.895 billion in the first three months of the year after ballooning 41 percent a year earlier.

"(It) is very much welcomed by the market. It provides a glimmer of hope that the first quarter GNP (gross national product, due out later this month) will not be that weak after all," said Manuel Goseco, chief economist of Dharmala Securities.
But analysts warned that the Philippines, with its long history of economic catastrophes, still had to prove itself to wary investors who are beginning to look a little tired of Southeast Asia.
"The crux of the issue is tax reform. If we do that, we will really show investors we can deliver," said Valenzuela, adding that the economic foundation of the country was sound.
For some analysts, the key could lie not just in economic growth but in the soundness of Philippine politics.
President Fidel Ramos, much feted by investors for turning around the economy, must under the constitution step down after his six-year term ends in 1998.
Several hopefuls are already jockeying for the job, but only one or two are judged likely to continue on the determined path of economic reform that Ramos has taken.
